title: A 20-minute weekly ops review that catches client-work slippage before the client does

sections.title: 30 seconds on who built this

  • I've audited delivery in dozens of $1-10M service businesses.

sections.title: Why this matters
sections.html:
Status lives in three people's heads and a Slack thread. You check a project when something feels off, or when a client pings you first. Both of those are lagging signals. By the time something *feels* off, the client already feels it too.

The math on getting this wrong is simple. One surprise churn at a mid account is $20k-$30k a year gone. Say you catch two of those a year with a Monday habit. That is $40k-$60k saved for the cost of 20 minutes a week, about 17 hours across the whole year.

A weekly review doesn't make you faster at delivery. It makes slippage visible on day 2 instead of day 9, while you can still fix it quietly.

sections.title: The order you check things in
sections.html:
Speed comes from a fixed order. You are not re-deciding what to look at each week, you are running the same pass every time. Same order, every account, top to bottom.

  1. Open the client engagement dashboard first, not the project itself. One row per active account, sorted by last activity. The oldest-activity accounts float to the top, and those are your suspects.
  2. Scan for the 6 flags on the top third of that list, the accounts that look quiet. A quiet account is either done or slipping, and you need to know which.
  3. Open the actual project only for accounts that tripped a flag. Everything green stays closed. This is the step that keeps 15-20 clients inside 20 minutes.
  4. Write one line per flagged account on the sheet as you go. Not later, as you go. The sheet is the output, the review is the input.
  5. Assign one next action per flagged account before you close it, with an owner and a day. A flag with no action is just anxiety.
If you open every project every week, you will run out of Monday before you run out of clients. The dashboard-first pass is what makes this scale past 8 accounts.

sections.title: The 6 slippage flags
sections.html:
These are the six things that mean an account is quietly slipping. If a row trips one, it goes on the sheet. Two or more flags on the same account means you call the owner today, not Monday.

#FlagWhat to look forWhy it means slippage
1Silent clientLast client-facing message is older than the cadence you promised themThe client is forming an opinion in the gap, and it is not a good one
2Passed due date, no status changeA deliverable's due date is behind us and the status still reads the same as last weekNobody moved it, which means nobody is on it
3Stuck in progressThe same task shows "in progress" across two reviews in a rowReal work moves states. A frozen state is a stall wearing a busy label
4Unanswered client questionA thread where the client asked something and the last message is theirsEvery hour here compounds. This is the flag that turns into the churn email
5Scope grew, timeline didn'tNew asks landed but the delivery date never movedYou are now behind by the size of the new ask, you just haven't admitted it yet
6Owner can't name the next milestoneThe account owner needs to open three tools to tell you what ships nextIf they can't say it fast, they are not steering it. They are reacting to it
Flags 1 and 4 are the expensive ones. Silence and an unanswered question are what the client actually feels. Flags 2, 3, 5, and 6 are the internal tells that predict flags 1 and 4 before the client sees them.

sections.title: The one-page review sheet
sections.html:
This is the sheet you fill in as you go. One block per flagged account, and only flagged accounts make it onto the page. Copy it into a Google Doc or a ClickUp doc view and reuse the same page every week so you build a slippage history per client.

The slipped 2 weeks running line at the bottom is the one that earns its keep. Any account that shows up flagged two Mondays in a row is a process problem, not a task problem, and it needs you, not a nudge.

sections.title: Running it in 20 minutes for 15-20 clients
sections.html:
The 20-minute number holds because most of your accounts are fine and you never open them. Here is where the time goes on a normal week with 3-4 flagged accounts.

StepWhat you doTime
Dashboard scanSort by last activity, eyeball the quiet third3 min
Flag passRun the 6 flags on the quiet accounts only5 min
Open flagged projectsOne at a time, confirm what's stuck8 min
Write the sheetOne block per flagged account, assign the action4 min
  • Time cost before: slippage surfaces when the client emails, usually 7-10 days late.
  • Time cost after: 20 minutes every Monday, slippage surfaces on day 2.
  • Break-even: one caught churn a year covers roughly 60 years of Mondays at $20k-$30k saved against 17 hours spent.
If your review is regularly running past 25 minutes, you are opening too many green accounts. Trust the dashboard sort. Closed-and-fine is the default, opening is the exception.

sections.title: What to do when a flag fires
sections.html:
A flag is not a to-do, it is a decision. For each flagged account, pick one of three moves before you close the block.

  • Fix it silently. The internal stall is real but the client hasn't felt it yet (flags 2, 3, 6). Reassign, unblock, done. No client message needed.
  • Get ahead of it. The client is about to feel it or already has (flags 1, 4). Send the proactive note today, before they send theirs. A heads-up you initiate reads as control. A reply to their chase reads as caught out.
  • Escalate it. Two or more flags, or a second week running. This is yours now. Call the owner, look at whether the account is scoped right, decide if the timeline needs a real reset with the client.
The whole point is that the client never gets to be the one who tells you. You want to be the person in the thread who moved first.
